patient.chief_complaint: Progressive memory problems and gait difficulty over the past several months
patient.history_present_illness: This 74-year-old right-handed woman, a retired elementary school teacher, presents to the neurology outpatient clinic with her daughter for evaluation of progressive cognitive decline and gait disturbance over approximately five months. The daughter first noticed subtle changes around five months ago when her mother began repeating the same questions within a single conversation and forgetting recent phone calls. Over the ensuing weeks, the patient reportedly missed several scheduled medical appointments, which was highly uncharacteristic of her previously meticulous organizational habits. Approximately three months ago the patient began having difficulty managing her household finances, resulting in several unpaid utility bills that the daughter discovered incidentally. The patient herself acknowledges some forgetfulness but minimizes the severity, attributing it to normal aging and poor sleep. Her daughter reports that the patient has become more socially withdrawn, declining invitations from longtime friends and spending more time at home alone. Approximately two months ago, the patient developed gait unsteadiness with several near-falls while walking in her apartment, prompting her to stop her daily walking routine. She has not had any witnessed falls with loss of consciousness or head trauma. She denies any episodes of urinary incontinence, visual hallucinations, or fluctuating levels of alertness. There have been no personality or behavioral changes, no compulsive behaviors, and no disinhibition noted by her daughter. The patient reports occasional word-finding difficulty in conversation, particularly when trying to recall names of acquaintances, though she remains conversational and coherent. She denies headaches, fever, night sweats, or unintentional weight loss. Sleep has been fragmented with frequent awakenings, but there is no history of dream-enactment behavior or restless legs. The patient's primary care physician checked basic labs three months ago and was told everything was normal, though her daughter is uncertain of the specific tests performed. No prior neuroimaging or cognitive testing has been done.

results.title: Differentiating idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus from Alzheimer's disease: a systematic review
results.key_finding: The classic NPH triad (gait disturbance, dementia, urinary incontinence) overlaps significantly with AD. Key differentiators include: disproportionate ventriculomegaly relative to sulcal enlargement (DESH sign) on MRI, gait improvement after large-volume lumbar puncture (tap test), and subcortical/frontal cognitive pattern in NPH versus amnestic pattern in AD.

results.title: Evans index and callosal angle in the diagnosis of normal pressure hydrocephalus
results.key_finding: Evans index >0.30 suggests ventriculomegaly. However, Evans index alone has limited specificity for NPH. Callosal angle <90 degrees is more specific for NPH. DESH (disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid-space hydrocephalus) pattern is the most reliable imaging criterion.

results.title: CSF biomarkers in NPH and AD: overlapping and distinguishing features
results.key_finding: NPH patients typically show normal or mildly decreased Abeta42 but normal tau levels, whereas AD patients show decreased Abeta42 with elevated tau and phospho-tau. Comorbid NPH and neurodegenerative pathology occurs in approximately 25-30% of elderly patients with ventriculomegaly.

output.summary: NPH and AD share overlapping clinical features, particularly in elderly patients with cognitive decline and gait disturbance. Key distinctions: (1) MRI findings - NPH shows disproportionate ventriculomegaly with crowded vertex sulci (DESH pattern), while AD shows proportional ventriculomegaly with cortical atrophy; (2) Cognitive pattern - NPH produces subcortical/frontal deficits while AD produces amnestic deficits; (3) CSF biomarkers - AD shows decreased Abeta42 with elevated tau, while NPH shows normal tau; (4) Tap test - clinical improvement after 30-50 mL CSF removal supports NPH. Comorbid pathology is common.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease (amnestic, multi-domain)

differential.key_features: DLB must be actively excluded by absence of visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, cognitive fluctuations, and REM sleep behavior disorder; biomarkers and (when needed) DaTscan can distinguish if features emerge
FTD typically presents with prominent personality change, disinhibition, or progressive aphasia rather than amnesia; positive amyloid biomarkers further argue against FTLD pathology
No significant cerebrovascular burden on MRI and the gradual amnestic course is not stepwise — pure VCI is unlikely
Insidious course over months to years with disproportionate delayed-recall impairment and limited benefit from cueing is not typical of pseudodementia

differential.diagnosis: Reversible metabolic, endocrine, or sleep-related cognitive impairment
differential.key_features: Screening labs exclude hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, and HIV; the progressive amnestic profile would not normalize with treatment of any of these alone

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed clinical history from patient and informant, including timeline, cognitive domains affected, functional decline, mood, sleep, and medication review
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Gradually progressive cognitive change with informant-confirmed functional impairment in IADLs

optimal_actions.action: Perform bedside cognitive assessment (MMSE and/or MoCA) and detailed neurological examination
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Objective cognitive impairment on MoCA more sensitive than MMSE; non-focal neurological exam (or variant-specific findings — visuospatial in PCA, language in lvPPA, behavioral in frontal AD)

optimal_actions.action: Order reversible-cause labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, vitamin B12, folate; consider RPR/HIV per risk)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible mimics (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis) excluded; identify and address co-morbid metabolic factors

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial-temporal atrophy and exclude vascular disease, hippocampal sclerosis, NPH, and mass lesions
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Subtle medial-temporal atrophy (Scheltens MTA grade 1-2) with or without temporoparietal volume loss

optimal_actions.action: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking

optimal_actions.action: Order amyloid PET when CSF biomarkers are unavailable or when diagnostic uncertainty persists after clinical assessment and MRI

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect / herniation risk, particularly in older patients

critical_actions: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate; HIV/RPR per risk)
Obtain structural brain MRI with dementia/volumetric protocol
Quantify cognitive impairment with a standardized cognitive battery (MoCA at minimum; formal neuropsychological testing when feasible)
Assess safety: driving, medication management, finances, and need for caregiver support
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives, and treatment options with the patient and family
Pursue biomarker confirmation (CSF AT(N) markers or amyloid PET) when MRI is equivocal or when an atypical AD variant is suspected
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risk
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioral indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia
Do not attribute symptoms entirely to normal aging, depression, or sleep apnea without completing the dementia workup
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage (memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD)
key_reasoning_points: MMSE may remain within the 'normal' range in highly educated patients with early AD; MoCA and formal neuropsychological testing are more sensitive at the MCI / mild dementia interface
The hallmark cognitive feature of AD is impaired delayed recall with rapid forgetting and limited benefit from cueing, reflecting a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit
APOE genotyping is a risk modifier and is not used to make the diagnosis; an E3/E4 or E4/E4 result is supportive but neither sufficient nor required for diagnosis
Low-normal B12 should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before being dismissed as a non-contributor
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line symptomatic therapy in mild-to-moderate AD; memantine is reserved for moderate-to-severe disease

red_herrings.data_point: Ventriculomegaly on MRI in a patient with memory and gait complaints
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on normal pressure hydrocephalus and pursue an LP / large-volume tap test as the primary intervention
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Ventriculomegaly is common with cortical atrophy in AD; NPH requires the full triad (gait, urinary, cognitive) with disproportionate ventricular enlargement relative to sulcal atrophy and a positive tap test — biomarkers and MRI pattern here support AD

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty due to overlapping features with NPH (ventriculomegaly, gait disturbance) and vascular cognitive impairment (white matter disease, prediabetic risk factors). The amnestic cognitive pattern and biomarker profile ultimately favor AD, but the diagnostic path requires systematic exclusion of NPH and reversible causes. Incidental prediabetic findings add a red herring vascular component.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Amnestic MCI with concurrent gait complaint and ventriculomegaly on MRI; NPH must be actively excluded
